name: Miles Pruett

biography.name: Miles Pruett

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; his grandfather visits for supper most Thursdays. Home routines are predictable, with room for disagreement.
background.finances: Comfortable income from accounting and insurance work; parents pay activity fees without difficulty but discuss purchases before buying.
background.geography: A suburban neighborhood outside McKinney, Texas; most destinations require a car.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking, multigenerational Texas family; holidays center on relatives rather than religious observance.
background.school: Large public high school; solid grades and no advanced-course expectations at home.
background.accessOpportunities: Has reliable internet and nearby community-college programs; has rarely explored beyond familiar activities.

timeline.story: At four, Miles arranged toy animals along the sofa while his sister invented their conversations. He liked repeating the same bedtime book and corrected his father when a familiar sentence was skipped.
In first grade he joined soccer because his neighbors did. He enjoyed the shared snacks and busier Saturdays more than matches, and his parents accepted his request to stop after two seasons.

His grandfather taught him to replace fishing line and keep a small tackle box orderly. Miles preferred untangling the equipment to waiting for fish, though he continued going for their conversations.
During remote school he completed assignments early and watched videos about unusual houses. A cardboard model occupied one weekend, but he abandoned it when the roof would not sit straight.

He volunteered at a library sale with his mother and discovered that sorting donations with an older volunteer felt easier than approaching strangers. He returned twice without being required to do so.

A friend invited him into theater crew. Miles liked painting flats and joking backstage, yet declined a larger responsibility when rehearsals conflicted with weekends at home and basketball with cousins. After a missed paint pickup delayed one rehearsal, he began checking supplies the day before. He disliked the mistake but appreciated that fixing it did not require becoming the loudest person in the room.

He now helps shelve books monthly and takes ordinary classes while friends discuss selective colleges. A recent campus visit felt pleasant but abstract; he remembers the cafeteria and workshop spaces better than the presentation.

ambitions: Unsure between community college and a four-year campus
Imagines an independent home with enough free evenings to see family.
struggles: Mistakes low urgency for having no interests

biography.selfDescription: I usually like things more once somebody gets me through the first day. Everyone thinks I must have a secret plan because I'm pretty calm, but I really don't have one yet.
openQuestions: Would a sustained project hold his attention?
Does he avoid leadership or the loss of free time?

response.branchReason: He returns to useful setup, shelving and surface painting with clear endpoints, making care of shared spaces a plausible practical introduction.
response.financialAssumptions: Independent housing and evenings with family are explicit wishes. A rental, used car and modest discretionary costs are reference assumptions. Current comfort is not translated into luxury aspiration.

Practical preparation and material organization appeal more than competitive achievement. Many unfamiliar domains receive middle responses because he has not explored them yet. Middle ratings for unfamiliar domains are tentative curiosity, not claims of experience.

Supply locations, instructions and appointments support familiar independent tasks. Laboratory methods and coding are new; ordinary reliability is not treated as global mastery. New/supported marks limited practice; an independent response describes a familiar task, not a measured aptitude.
Steady mixed work and family time fit his present preferences. He explicitly compares community college and a four-year campus, both covered by college.
